Improving Graph-as-Policy · Bosch · NVIDIA · UC Berkeley

Perception that doesn't abort

A drop-in change to GaP (Graph-as-Policy) that fixes its single biggest failure mode — the perception node that gives up. On the cream-cheese-box task it turns 25% into 87.5%, and every line of it is opt-in and reversible.

01 The result — one node, one change

GaP's task success is often gated by one perception node. On LIBERO task 1 (“pick up the cream cheese box, put it in the basket”) the object-identification node keeps failing, routing the graph to not_found → abort before the arm ever moves. Our change fixes exactly that node.

Why the step count is the proof. A baseline trial dies after ~192 steps — the graph reached perceive, couldn't pick the object, and aborted before the arm moved. With our change the same task runs ~749 steps — perception succeeds, so the arm actually grasps and places. The failure-attribution tool confirms it independently: 100% of baseline failures are perception, the exact mode we target. (Measured on the real GaP benchmark, 8 trials/arm, Gemini-3.1-pro codegen + Gemini-flash-lite perception. See the honest read.)

02 What GaP is — a policy you can read

GaP (Graph-as-Policy) is a multi-agent harness that compiles a language instruction into a typed, verified skill graph and executes it unchanged in sim or on a real robot. A policy is “a directed computation graph of atomic nodes joined by data and control edges — interpretable, modular, reusable” — inspired by ROS graphs and TAMP. An orchestration agent partitions the task and dispatches skill agents that synthesize localized subgraphs from the MORSL library (51 skills: perception, grasp/motion planning, 2D/3D vision, verification), and every edge is statically type-checked. A self-learning loop rehearses the graph in simulation, localizes failures to specific nodes, and edits topology and parameters until performance plateaus (e.g. Make-Popcorn 33% → 94% in sim).

┌─ 1. TASK (natural language) ────────────────────────────────────────┐
   "Pick up the cream cheese box and put it in the basket."
└─────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ▼   multi-agent codegen (Gemini-3.1-pro), edges type-checked
┌─ 2. SKILL GRAPH  (workflow.json — a DAG of MORSL subgraphs) ─────────┐
   target_sg    : observe → perceive → filter_obb → found ──not_found──┐
   container_sg : observe → perceive → filter_obb → found ──not_found──┤
   grasp_sg     : open → compute_grasp → goto_grasp → observe → close   │
   transport_sg : transport_move → release → placed                     │
                              │                                         ▼
                              ▼                                    abort  (arm home)
                            done
└─────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ▼   tool servers: grounding-dino · sam3 · vlm · curobo · geometry
┌─ 3. EXECUTE on LIBERO (MuJoCo, 20 Hz) → reward ∈ {0, 1} ─────────────┘

Materials: project page · paper (arXiv 2607.05369) · graph-as-policy · open-robot-skills. The explicit graph is exactly what makes our fix possible: we can see which node fails and improve only that one, instead of treating the task as a black box.

03 The bottleneck — the perception tournament

Every perceive node runs the same script: Grounding-DINO proposes candidate boxes from a broad "object." prompt, a VLM tournament (pairwise “A or B?”) picks which box is the target, then SAM3 segments it. The tournament exists for a reason — for tiny objects, a 2-way comparison is far more reliable than asking a VLM to pick 1-of-N. But it has two costs.

① Accuracy
not_found
② Efficiency
~14 calls

① On the cream-cheese-box the tournament loses. The flat white-and-blue box is hard, and the arm/basket distractors are in the bracket — the VLM can’t pin it down, so the graph exits not_found → abort and the arm never moves (the ~51–192-step deaths above). ② It’s also the latency centre: the tournament is O(N) sequential VLM API calls — with two perceive nodes per episode, one episode makes ~14 VLM round-trips, even though only one box ever reaches SAM3.

04 Our fix — a difficulty-adaptive perception budget

The insight: the accuracy fix and the efficiency fix are the same change. Before the tournament, we pre-rank the candidate boxes against the target (a second Grounding-DINO pass with the specific object name — no new model), prune the ones that match nothing (the arm and basket score ~0), and skip the tournament entirely when the top candidate is clearly ahead. The number of VLM calls then scales with scene difficulty instead of being fixed.

What you just watched. The target-name pass gives the real box a high score (~0.62) and the arm/basket/fragment a score of 0.0 — they’re removed before the VLM ever sees them. On an easy scene the confidence gate fires and the tournament is skipped (0 calls); on a hard one it runs over 2–3 boxes instead of 7. Same pairwise reliability, a fraction of the calls, and the distractors that cause not_found can no longer win.

# opt-in, default off — baseline is byte-identical unless set
export GAP_PERCEPTION_PRERANK=dino      # pre-rank candidates vs the target name
export GAP_PERCEPTION_TOPK=3            # keep the top-k before the tournament
export GAP_PERCEPTION_SKIP_MARGIN=0.25  # skip the VLM entirely when confident

05 Two more improvements to the same node

Repair instead of abort — and an honest negative

The idea: on a not_found, re-run perception with escalating recall (the specific target prompt, then relaxed thresholds) before signalling abort — a local repair of the failed node (GAP_PERCEPTION_REPAIR=on, opt-in). On task 1 it did nothing — and that turns out to be informative. In our A/B the repair fired 0 times: task-1's perception never returns a clean not_found — it returns a wrong-but-confident pick (or the not-found is decided by a downstream node), which repair's trigger never sees. So repair is aimed at a different failure mode — a genuine missed detection — than the one task 1 has. The clean negative is itself a result: it proves task 1 is a “wrong-pick” problem (which pre-ranking fixes at the source), not a “missed-detection” one. To make repair earn its keep, it needs a different trigger (fire on a low-confidence pick, or at the graph's downstream not-found edge) or a task where Grounding-DINO truly misses the object.

Failure attribution

A small tool reads a benchmark run and attributes each task’s failures to graph-generation / perception / execution — from control-step counts and workflow validity. On our A/B it reported baseline task-1 failures as 100% perception (and 0% for our run), independently confirming what the pre-ranking targets.

task   succ%   steps  fails  stage          # baseline run, real output
1      25.0%    192      6    perception     →  perception 6/6 (100%)

06 The A/B, on the real benchmark

Three arms, plus pre-ranking on its own — all on task 1, 8 trials each, perception cache off, on the real GaP LIBERO benchmark (2×4090). Firing counts are logged directly from the perception node.

Task-1 · cream cheese box (8 trials)successavg stepsfiring
Baseline GaP (unchanged)2/8 = 25.0%192—
Repair only (Goal 2)2/8 = 25.0%192repair 0×
Pre-ranking (Goal 1, ours)7/8 = 87.5%749prerank 24×
Pre-ranking + Repair (combined)7/8 = 87.5%750prerank 24×, repair 0×

The story is clean: pre-ranking (Goal 1) is the causal fix (25% → 87.5%, fired 24×), and adding repair on top doesn't hurt (87.5%). Repair on its own does nothing — for the reason below, which is itself a useful finding.

07 The honest read

What this is, and what it isn’t This is a real, causal improvement on the perception-bottleneck task: 2/8 → 7/8, the mechanism confirmed active (fired 24×), the step-count signature flipped (abort → execute), and the attribution tool independently localizing baseline failures to perception. What it isn’t yet: the full 10-task gate average — this is one task at n = 8, with baseline and ours on different generated graphs, so the exact magnitude will move with more trials. The next step is the same A/B across the other tasks for a per-task before/after. Every change is opt-in and default-off (baseline byte-identical), lives in the existing perceiving-objects/perceive_dino_vlm.py node, and is fully reversible.

Built on GaP — Graph-as-Policy (Chen et al.; Bosch · NVIDIA · UC Berkeley). Improvements & measurements are our own; all numbers are from the real GaP LIBERO benchmark on 2×RTX 4090.
